newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian resources move to fore as banks retreat.
newsitem.headline: Australian resources move to fore as banks retreat.

text.p: Leading resource stocks look set to take over the star role from banks on the Australian share market for a time as world growth prospects lure investors to the key commodity stocks, analysts said on Tuesday.
"There is no question the economic fundamentals are very friendly to resource equities," said Dennis Mahoney, chief economist at Prudential-Bache Securities (Australia) Ltd.
Resources extended their recent rally on Tuesday and sector benchmark, the All Resources Index, hit a year high of 1,488.1 on Tuesday for a 9.3 percent jump in a month.

"We have had some good numbers out of Japan and less so out of Germany but all of a sudden it looks like, if it is not synchronised growth, it is the next best thing which is growth rates in industrial production moving up together," Mahoney said.

In the last three days alone, the indicator has added just over four percent to today's high as the underlying switch to commodity stocks accelerated on a flight by funds from the margin-pressured banking sector.

Leading the charge since May 15 has been market bellwether The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, up 6.2 percent to A$19.25, diversified miner CRA Ltd, up 5.4 percent to A$21.11, and gold and nickel major WMC Ltd, up 6.5 percent to A$8.38.

"There was obviously some switching going on with profit taking in the banks and that is pretty understandable," said dealer Michael Sichlau of Daiwa Securities, noting the tougher outlook for the previously invincible "Big Four" banks.

Despite substantial first half profit rises, Westpac Banking Corp and sector leader National Australia Bank Ltd warned last week of competitive domestic trading conditions with subsequent pressures on margins.
While the resources index rocketed in the last three days, the banking index lost 3.8 percent and Daiwa's Sichlau warned there could be more to come with a further flow on to the resource leaders.
"There is obviously still some profits in the banks to be taken so it might continue. We just have to wait and see," he said.

Prudential-Bache's Mahoney agreed the coincidence of bad news for the banks and a switch in sector weighting had accelerated the rise, suggesting what may have been a more restrained rally over a longer period had been compressed.
"The fact that it has happened in two days is a little breathtaking," Mahoney said.

"When resources run, they only run for a few months so we have already basically had a month of resources outperforming the industrials," he added, noting that the key commodity stocks were a logical choice for funds freed up by the banking selloff. "Where do you go if you don't stay in the banks? You try the cyclicals and of course the renowned cyclicals are the resources, given that the fundamentals look good."

The growth outlook was likely to continue underpinning strength in commodity stocks, with even a modest reduction in growth among the G-7 economies unlikely to severely dent the trend to commodity driven stocks.

"Even if we are misreading the Japanese economy, I think there is enough strength in the U.S., Japan and Europe put together to say the risk is that commodity prices will move up more than most analysts are expecting," Mahoney said.
"So on that basis I think this move up is justified."
